correctness.rationale: Independently verified the normalized reciprocal-coordinate analysis. For a+b+c=1 and abc nonzero the rational tangent coefficients are 3−1/a, 3−1/b, 3−1/c; the common Gauss direction parameter reduces to a cubic with roots 0 (excluded singular point) and 1 (the starting point), and a single remaining linear factor with coefficient 3D0−2R0 and constant −3D0. That factor cannot vanish identically at a smooth point: R0=D0=0 gives (a,b,c)=(1/3,1/3,1/3) by the elementary symmetric polynomials. Denominator zeros and coincidences with 0 or 1 give exactly R∪D∪H using the displayed factor identities. On the node lines [x:y:z]=[w+Ut:w+Vt:w], the restriction of D is t²[2(U²−UV+V²)w+UV(U+V)t]; the two coefficients have no common projective zero, including directions 0,−1,∞. The residual point is the node on exactly the rational node directions, so the point counts q or q+2 are valid over extension fields. On x=y=a,z=b, R=(a−b)² and D=2a(a−b)²; on x=a,y=a+t,z=a−t, R=3t² and D=6at². These check disjointness with H off the excluded node and boundary. The split R lines have four distinct boundary points because R is nonzero at all six boundary intersections; each H line has three distinct boundary points. The six boundary points on D are obtained by restrictions to x=0 and x+y+z=0. Summing the disjoint counts and using the smooth-locus cardinality (q−1)(q−2) proves both formulas. The broken display of some nonzero signs is typographical: the intended exclusion xyz(x+y+z)=0 is explicit in the boundary count and in the cited source.
correctness.reproduction: Read the bundled artifacts/verify.py (prime-field regression and exact polynomial identities; not executed). As an additional independent exact witness, enumerated a,b in F=F_p[t]/(t²−d) for (p,d)=(5,2),(7,3), kept abc≠0 for c=1−a−b, discarded the zero tangent vector, and counted reciprocal tangent triples normalized by the first nonzero entry. Obtained (N1,N2)=(192,180) for q=25 and (408,924) for q=49. The proof, not these witnesses, gives the prime-power theorem.
